title: Walking
body:
Walking is the human baseline: about 1.4 meters per second, a comfortable adult pace on level ground, the speed at which a person covers roughly five kilometers in an hour and at which every detail of the ground can be watched as it passes.

Reference speed: 1.4 m/s. Time to cover 100 km at this speed: 19.84 hours; time to cover the Earth-Moon distance at this speed: 8700.64 years; time to cover one astronomical unit: 3386098.53 years.

Its limit is the body: hills, loads, and fatigue cut it quickly, and no walker sustains even this pace for a full day. It is the reference against which every faster machine is measured in this simulator. Standard math: c = 299,792,458 m/s is the absolute limit; this reference is far below c, so time dilation is negligible for it, and the simulator's near-c rows carry the dilation factors.

title: Bicycle

title: Voyager Probe
body:
The Voyager probes cruise at about 17,000 meters per second, the fastest objects humans have ever launched, coasting on gravity assists and their own momentum through interstellar space, still sending signals home after decades.

Reference speed: 17000.0 m/s. Time to cover 100 km at this speed: 5.88 seconds; time to cover the Earth-Moon distance at this speed: 261.71 days; time to cover one astronomical unit: 278.86 years.

Its limit is that it is coasting, not powered: no engine now pushes it, and its speed is a gift from Jupiter's and Saturn's gravity, not a throttle a traveler can set. It stands for the fastest thing we have actually built. title: Light in Vacuum
body:
Light in vacuum travels at 299,792,458 meters per second, exactly, the speed denoted c, the fastest speed at which any signal, object, or information can travel, and the absolute limit of this simulator and of physics as currently understood.

Reference speed: 299792458.0 m/s. Time to cover 100 km at this speed: 333.564 microseconds; time to cover the Earth-Moon distance at this speed: 21.37 minutes; time to cover one astronomical unit: 5.78 days.

Its limit is the law itself: no massive object reaches c, and as speed approaches c, time dilation grows without bound, so a traveler's clock slows relative to stay-at-home clocks. This row is the standard against which every other row is measured. Standard math: c = 299,792,458 m/s is the absolute limit; this reference is far below c, so time dilation is negligible for it, and the simulator's near-c rows carry the dilation factors.

title: One Hundred Kilometers
body:
One hundred kilometers is a city-to-city hop: a walk of a day, a bicycle ride of hours, a highway drive of about an hour, a jet flight of minutes, and for light, a third of a millisecond, a blink's tiny fraction.

Distance: 100,000 km. Walking it takes 2.26 years; a highway car takes 38.58 days; a passenger jet takes 4.63 days; light takes 333.564 milliseconds, which is the one-way light-time delay for this distance.

This distance is chosen because every reference in the table gives a human-scale answer for it, from a day down to a fraction of a millisecond, so the whole table can be read at a glance. Standard math: the full simulator table rebuilds these times for every reference when the distance or the reference changes, and near-c rows show time dilation per special relativity, gamma = 1/sqrt(1-v^2/c^2).

title: Earth's Circumference
body:
Earth's circumference at the equator is about 40,075 kilometers: a walk around the world would take years, a jet about two days of flying, and light about one seventh of a second, circling the planet seven and a half times per second.

Distance: 40,075,000 km. Walking it takes 907.07 years; a highway car takes 42.33 years; a passenger jet takes 5.08 years; light takes 2.23 minutes, which is the one-way light-time delay for this distance.

This distance makes the planet's size concrete: it is the largest distance that still belongs to one world, and the point where even jets need days and only light is fast. title: Earth to the Moon
body:
Earth to the Moon is about 384,400 kilometers: Apollo took about three days at rocket speeds, a jet would need about eighteen days of continuous flight, a walker about nine years, and light about 1.3 seconds, the delay every lunar conversation must pay.

Distance: 384,400,000 km. Walking it takes 8700.64 years; a highway car takes 406.03 years; a passenger jet takes 48.72 years; light takes 21.37 minutes, which is the one-way light-time delay for this distance.

This distance is the first true space distance, and its light-time delay is the reason Moon missions are flown by plan and program, not by joystick. title: Earth to Mars at Closest
body:
Earth to Mars at closest approach is about 55 million kilometers: a fast probe takes about seven months, light takes about three minutes, and a jet would need about twenty-five years of continuous flight, which is why Mars is a voyage, not a trip.

Distance: 55,000,000,000 km. Walking it takes 1244889.16 years; a highway car takes 58094.83 years; a passenger jet takes 6971.38 years; light takes 2.12 days, which is the one-way light-time delay for this distance.

This distance changes with the planets' orbits, from about 55 million to over 400 million kilometers, so the table for it is a best-case figure, and the simulator states that plainly. title: Earth to the Sun (1 AU)
body:
One astronomical unit, Earth to the Sun, is about 149.6 million kilometers: light takes about eight minutes and twenty seconds to cross it, so the Sun we see is always eight minutes old, and a probe at Voyager's speed would need about seventeen years.

Distance: 149,600,000,000 km. Walking it takes 3386098.53 years; a highway car takes 158017.93 years; a passenger jet takes 18962.15 years; light takes 5.78 days, which is the one-way light-time delay for this distance.

This distance is the solar system's yardstick: every other planetary distance is measured in units of it, and its light-time is the reason solar weather is forecast, never watched live.
